subject: STAN does not work well for models with large number of parameters

messages.author: 614b5e0181ba03ae
messages.subject: STAN does not work well for models with large number of parameters
parts:
Hi all,

I have troubles of fitting this model (at the end of this post) effectively. The model has 1010 parameters (my actual model has 8000+ parameters...). The parameters are nicely estimated when I set a specific seed number in function sampling(). If I change to any other seed number or do not specify it, the chains do not move at all even if I set adapt_delta extremely close to 1. As shown in the sampling() function below, I only reset adapt_deta and max_treedepth under "control", and all the rest arguments under "control" are kept at their default values.

My question is: which arguments can I change in order to improve the sampler performance (i.e. make the chains move)? In the model below, luckily I've found a certain seed number which makes the sampler works fine. But this is after I've run the model for so many times. My actual model has a much larger number of parameters, and I guess it will take me forever to find the right seed number for my actual model... I've made adapt_delta as large as I can, but it didn't help much.
Any suggestions/tips?? Or did I wrote my model in such a way that STAN is not able to run efficiently? Thanks.

## test the AR(1) model ##
library(rstan)
A <- 20
B <- 25
E <- 5
N <- A * B
a_n <- rep(1:A, each = B)
b_n <- rep(1:B, times = A)
e_n <- rep(E:1, each = N/E)
pri_rho_lower <- 0
pri_rho_upper <- 1
pri_sigma_eps_lower <- 0
pri_sigma_eps_upper <- 0.05
pri_sigmas_lower <- 0
pri_sigmas_upper <- 2
pri_nu_lower <- 3
pri_nu_upper <- 50
X_lower <- log(0.5)
X_upper <- log(2)

set.seed(1234)
logy <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 0.05)

test_data <- list(A = A, B = B, N = N, E = E,
                  logy = logy,
                  a_n = a_n, b_n = b_n, e_n = e_n,
                  X_lower = X_lower, X_upper = X_upper,
                  pri_sigmas_lower = pri_sigmas_lower,
                  pri_sigmas_upper = pri_sigmas_upper,
                  pri_nu_lower = pri_nu_lower,
                  pri_nu_upper = pri_nu_upper,
                  pri_rho_lower = pri_rho_lower,
                  pri_rho_upper = pri_rho_upper,
                  pri_sigma_eps_lower = pri_sigma_eps_lower,
                  pri_sigma_eps_upper = pri_sigma_eps_upper)

test_model1 <- "
data {
int<lower=1> A;
int<lower=1> B;
int<lower=1> N;
int<lower=1> E;
int<lower=1, upper=A> a_n[N];
int<lower=1, upper=B> b_n[N];
int<lower=1, upper=E> e_n[N];
real logy[N];
real X_lower;
real X_upper;
real<lower=0> pri_rho_lower;
real<lower=0> pri_rho_upper;
real<lower=0> pri_sigma_eps_lower;
real<lower=0> pri_sigma_eps_upper;
real<lower=1> pri_nu_lower;
real<lower=1> pri_nu_upper;
real<lower=0> pri_sigmas_lower;
real<lower=0> pri_sigmas_upper;
}//end of data

parameters {
matrix[A,B] Z_ab;
real<lower=pri_rho_lower, upper=pri_rho_upper> rho;
real<lower=pri_sigma_eps_lower, upper=pri_sigma_eps_upper> sigma_eps;
real<lower=pri_sigmas_lower, upper=0.05> sigma_e[E];
real<lower=pri_nu_lower, upper=pri_nu_upper> nu;
}//end of parameters

transformed parameters {
matrix<lower=X_lower, upper=X_upper>[A,B] X_ab;
real<lower=0> sigma_eps_stat;
sigma_eps_stat <- sqrt(sigma_eps^2 / (1 - rho^2));

for (a in 1:A) {
X_ab[a, 1] <- X_lower + inv_logit(sigma_eps_stat * Z_ab[a, 1]) * (X_upper - X_lower);
for (b in 2:B) {
X_ab[a, b] <- X_lower +
inv_logit(rho * X_ab[a, b-1] + sigma_eps * Z_ab[a, b]) * (X_upper - X_lower);
}//end of b loop
}//end of a loop
}//end of transformed parameters

model {
rho ~ uniform(pri_rho_lower, pri_rho_upper);
sigma_eps ~ uniform(pri_sigma_eps_lower, pri_sigma_eps_upper);
nu ~ uniform(pri_nu_lower, pri_nu_upper);
sigma_e ~ uniform(pri_sigmas_lower, pri_sigmas_upper);

for (a in 1:A)
for (b in 1:B)
Z_ab[a, b] ~ student_t(nu, 0, 1);
// data model //
for (n in 1:N) {
logy[n] ~ normal(X_ab[a_n[n], b_n[n]], sqrt(0.05^2 + sigma_e[e_n[n]]^2));
}//end of n loop
}//end of model
"

fit_test1 <- sampling(
  object = stan_model(model_code = test_model1),
  data = test_data,
  seed = 1973597442, #this seed works when A=20, B=25
  control = list(
    # adapt_gamma: default=0.05
    adapt_gamma = 0.05,
    # adapt_kappa: default=0.8
    adapt_kappa = 0.8,
    # adapt_t0: default=10
    adapt_t0 = 10,
    # adapt_init_buffer: default=75
    adapt_init_buffer = 75,
    # adapt_term_buffer: default=50
    adapt_term_buffer = 50,
    # adapt_window: default=25
    adapt_window = 25,
    # adapt_delta: target acceptance probability; default=0.8; max=0.9999999999999999444222
    adapt_delta = 0.9999999999999999444222,
    # max_treedepth: should increase if adapt_delta is high; default=10.
    max_treedepth = 100),
  iter = 1000, chains = n_chains, warmup = 2)


## trace plot
traceplot(fit_test1,
          par = c(dimnames(fit_test1)[[3]][sample(1:dim(fit_test1)[3], size = 4)],
                  paste0("sigma_e", "[", 1:E, "]"),
                  "rho", "sigma_eps", "nu"))

messages.subject: Re: STAN does not work well for models with large number of parameters
parts:
I can say with confidence that it's not the number of parameters as I'm working with a model that has about 13k parameters and it runs in about an hour.  The lack of indentation in your pasted code makes it hard to read but Z_ab should probably be re-parameterized (it's currently a t-distributed parameter, you can keep the distribution but create it using a transformed parameter---it's been discussed on list) you also have a state-space AR model which there was some talk about working better with a non-centered parameterization.  The lack of indendation makes the model hard to read for me so I'll stop there.  If you can't find the re-parameterizations, ask a separate question with a better subject.

Krzysztof

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] STAN does not work well for models with large number of parameters
parts:
Usually tightly constrained, non-unit-scaled parameters are
difficult:

Warmup is going to need to find the scale to move sigma_e.

You don't need uniform distributions explicitly if the constraints
match. And if the constraints don't match, you'll have bigger problems.
For instance, this is inconsistent:

...

sigma_e ~ uniform(pri_sigmas_lower, pri_sigmas_upper);

unless pri_sigmas_upper = 0.05. Every variable value that satisifies
the constraint should have support in the model (note that the converse
is not necessary).

You also have some implicit transforms, like

where the .05^2 is going to be some tiny increment to sigma_e, which is
already bounded by pri_sigmas_lower. I think it'd be easier to just put
the constraint you care about on sigma_e and then put a prior on the
constrained variable.

And finally some general advice: work up to more complicated models with
simpler models to start. Finally, this is going to be problematic numrically:

adapt_delta = 0.9999999999999999444222,

Floating-point precision just isn't that high, so that number overflows to 1,
which requires every single state to be accepted, which is probably causing
a ridiculously small step size.

- Bob
